Date: 2023-03-22
REMARKS
New dependent claims 149-151 have been added and are supported by the specification as filed, for example, on page 18, lines 18-20 and page 25, line 9. No new matter has been added.
Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, and 147-151 are now pending for examination with claim 1 being independent.
Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in View of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai
Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-138, 140-144, 147, and 148 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 to Rylander et al. ("Rylander") in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2005/0161594 to Hollingsworth et al. ("Hollingsworth"), U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2011/0208031 to Wolfe et al. ("Wolfe"), and U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2011/0207237 to Sai et al. ("Sai").
The Examiner alleges that Rylander teaches each and every feature of independent claim 1, except for: (i) the end portion having a diameter of less than 100 nm, which the Examiner alleges is taught by Hollingsworth (see page 5, last paragraph of the Office Action dated November 22, 2022); (ii) at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, which the Examiner alleges is taught by Wolfe (see page 6, first paragraph of the Office Action); and (iii) the at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member is configured to facilitate analysis of the cell, which the Examiner alleges is taught by Sai (see page 7, last paragraph of the Office Action). The Examiner alleges that it would have been obvious for a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai, and that there would have been a reasonable expectation of success in doing so (see page 8, first paragraph of the Office Action). However, it is believed that this rejection is deficient and should be withdrawn for at least the following reasons.
I. Rylander fails to teach or suggest a member having an end portion having a diameter of less than 100 nm, and teaches away from: (i) an end portion being configured for insertion into a cell while maintaining viability of the cell; and (ii) an end portion of less than 100 nm, as the member would not have sufficient structural integrity when penetrating through the skin.
Initially, it is noted that the Examiner agrees that Rylander fails to teach or suggest an end portion having a diameter of less than 100 nm (see page 5 of the Office Action). Indeed, it is not surprising that Rylander fails to teach or suggest a member comprising an end portion having a diameter of less than 100 nm, since Rylander is not concerned with maintaining the viability of a single cell. Instead, Rylander is directed to systems configured to perform cancer therapy in the skin by penetrating the skin and inducing photothermal or photochemical damage to target tissue. The skin is much thicker than an individual cell, and is further composed of dead cells, and thus Rylander is not concerned with keeping skin cells alive.
Rylander discloses, for example, systems for delivering exogenous photoabsorbers such as nanoparticles (e.g., single-wall carbon nanohorns or SWNHs) to tissue regions for targeted cancer treatment (e.g., destruction) of cancer cells (see, for example, paragraphs [0295]-[0300] of Rylander). In particular, paragraph [0299] of Rylander states, "The present invention discloses the ability to add targeting molecules to the SWNHs and shown selective photothermal destruction of tumor cells." In addition, paragraph [0300] of Rylander states, "The present invention discloses the ability to destroy tumor cells when laser irradiation at 1064 nm was used in combination with SWNHs."
The tips of the microneedles in Rylander are relatively thick in diameter, which is necessary due to Rylander's goal of physically penetrating multiple layers of skin and delivering light directly into a target area below the skin surface (see, for example, the Abstract and paragraphs [0171] and [0172] in conjunction with FIGS. 3A-3C of Rylander). Accordingly, such microneedles, due to the fact that they must penetrate through multiple layers of the skin (e.g., the epidermis and the dermis), are required to be both relatively long and relatively thick (e.g., to have sufficient structural integrity when penetrating through the skin). Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would not have modified the microneedles in Rylander to have cross-sectional diameters of less than 100 nm. See M.P.E.P. § 2143.01(V) (The Proposed Modification Cannot Render the Prior Art Unsatisfactory For Its Intended Purpose).
As evidenced by Makvandi, P., et al., Nano-Micro Lett., 2021, 13, 93 ("Makvandi"), submitted herewith, microneedles, such as those described in Rylander, must be configured to pierce the human stratum corneum (-10 to 20 micrometers, formed of mostly dead cells) without rupturing or bending during penetration (see, for example, the Abstract of Makvandi). As shown in Tables 3 and 4 of Rylander, respectively, the flat microneedles in Rylander have a tip diameter ranging from 9-139 micrometers, while the sharp microneedles in Rylander have a tip diameter ranging from 2-8 micrometers. The smallest tip diameter disclosed in Rylander (i.e., 2 micrometers) is therefore more than an order of magnitude larger than the less than 100 nm diameter of the end portion as recited in independent claim 1.
Also submitted herewith is Waghule, T., et al., Biomed. Pharmacother., 2019, 109, 3, 1249- 1258 ("Waghule"), which is a review article describing microneedles that are used for transdermal administration of drugs (see, for example, the Abstract of Waghule). Section 5 of Waghule describes the different types of transdermal microneedles in the literature, including solid microneedles, coated microneedles, dissolving microneedles, hollow microneedles, and hydrogel- forming microneedles (see, for example, pages 1251-1253 of Waghule). The microneedles described in Rylander are examples of hollow microneedles (see, for example, paragraphs [0029] and [0152] of Rylander). Waghule describes the dimensions of transdermal microneedles in Section 3, and discloses that the transdermal microneedles have a 1-25 micrometer tip thickness (see, for example, page 1250 of Waghule).
In addition, submitted herewith is Davis, S.P., et al., J. Biomech., 2004, 37, 1155-1163 ("Davis"), which describes the force required to insert microneedles into living skin and the force needles can withstand before fracturing (see, for example, the Abstract of Davis). Davis tested microneedles with a tip radius of 30-80 micrometers (see, for example, page 1157, right column, first full paragraph of Davis). Davis further discloses "[i]n the case of tip radius, both modeling approaches predict a moderate increase in fracture force with increasing tip radius," i.e., the force required to fracture microneedles increases with increasing tip radius (see, for example, the Abstract and the paragraph bridging pages 1161-1162 of Davis). The state of the art therefore describes transdermal microneedles having a tip diameter of at least 1 micrometer, and that microneedles with smaller tip diameters require less force to fracture as compared to microneedles with larger tip diameters.
The Examiner alleges that the end portion in Rylander is "capable" of performing the function of being inserted into a cell while maintaining viability of the cell, since a human egg and a hen egg are single cells having diameters of 130 micrometers and 43 millimeters, respectively (see page 4 of the Office Action). There is no teaching or suggestion in Rylander, however, that the microneedles disclosed therein could have been modified in such a way as to maintain viability of a cell, whether the cell is a human egg, a hen egg, or a HeLa cell, instead of inducing photothermal or photochemical damage in the skin.
It should be noted that the dimensions in Rylander and as claimed differ by an order of magnitude, and the Examiner identifies no rational reason why one of ordinary skill in the art would have made the tip of the microneedle in Rylander smaller, while the state of the art teaches away from using smaller dimensions. For example, page 25, lines 9-26 of the specification as filed in conjunction with FIG. 4E describes that a fiber tip probe (FTP) having a tip diameter in the micrometer range (e.g., 5 micrometers) causes cell death after puncturing the cell, while a fiber tip probe having a tip diameter less than 100 nm maintains cell viability. In addition, as evidenced by Kim, W., et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2007, 129, 7228-7229 ("Kim"), submitted herewith, the viability of cells shows strong dependence on the size of nanowires used to pierce the cells. When large diameter (-400 nm) nanowires were used, cell death occurred within a day, whereas small diameter (-30 nm) nanowires preserved cell life for more than 5 days (see, for example, the paragraph bridging pages 7228 and 7229 of Kim). Furthermore, Ryu, S., et al., J. Biosci. Bioeng., 2013, 116, 3, 391-396 ("Ryu"), also submitted herewith, states that insertion of a nanoneedle 200 nm in diameter has no significant effect on cell viability even after 1 hour of insertion (see, for example, page 394, first full paragraph of Ryu).
Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would have known, based on such references, that larger diameters are preferable if the goal is to kill cells, as Rylander teaches. Accordingly, because Rylander teaches microneedles that are configured to destroy tumor cells and have a tip diameter of at least 2 micrometers configured to penetrate layers of skin, Rylander teaches away from microneedles having diameters of less than 100 nm that are configured to maintain viability of a cell, as recited in independent claim 1.
II. A person of ordinary skill would have had no motivation or rational reason to combine Rylander and Hollingsworth.
The Examiner alleges that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have had motivation to combine Rylander and Hollingsworth with a reasonable expectation of success since Hollingsworth teaches it is well-known in the art for near-field scanning optical microscopes to comprise an optical fiber having a tapered end with a diameter of about 100 nm, and Rylander and Hollingsworth both teach a member configured to guide and/or direct light (see pages 5-6 of the Office Action).
However, although Rylander and Hollingsworth are indeed both directed to optical probes, they are used for very different applications. As described above, the microneedles in Rylander are directed to light-based therapeutics for penetration of tissue to deliver light directly to a target area below the skin (see, for example, the Abstract of Rylander). In contrast, Hollingsworth is generally directed to a plasmon enhanced near-field optical probe that is configured to analyze samples ex situ. See, for example, paragraph [0043] in conjunction with FIG. 2 of Hollingsworth, which discloses that the near-field scanning optical microscope 50 includes a stage 80 on which a sample 82 is placed, which allows a user to view an area of the sample 82 adjacent to the plasmon enhanced near-field optical probe 10. Hollingsworth further requires a microscope cantilever having a lever arm with an aperture, a tip to provide tip-to-sample separation feedback, and a plasmon enhancement structure (see, for example, the Abstract of Hollingsworth).
Indeed, Hollingsworth does not mention "needle" or "skin" and is wholly directed to the analysis of ex situ samples, not to the delivery of light and photoabsorbers into the skin. For this reason alone, there would have been no motivation for a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify a transdermal microneedle configured to deliver light below the surface of skin, as disclosed by Rylander, with a near-field scanning optical microscope configured to analyze samples ex situ, as disclosed by Hollingsworth. Furthermore, Hollingsworth requires a cantilevered arm, and it is not clear how such a cantilevered arm could function while it is attached to a probe inserted into the skin, as required by Rylander.
In view of the above, a person of ordinary skill in the art, looking to modify Rylander, would most certainly look to the plethora of literature describing transdermal microneedles (e.g., Makvandi, Waghule, and Davis, as previously discussed), not to the disclosure of Hollingsworth directed to near-field scanning optical microscopes for the ex-situ analysis of samples. The Examiner fails to explain why one of ordinary skill in the art would instead have chosen Hollingsworth, rather than references relating to penetrating skin and delivering light below the skin surface. Furthermore, modifying the microneedle in Rylander with Hollingsworth, as proposed by the Examiner, would have rendered Rylander unsatisfactory for its intended purpose of physically penetrating tissue and delivering light directly into a target area below the skin surface. See M.P.E.P. § 2143.01(V). Thus, it is submitted that the combination of Rylander and Hollingsworth is improper.
III. Wolfe fails to teach or suggest at least one particle attached to the end portion of a member via an adhesive.
The Examiner alleges that Wolfe teaches at least one particle attached to the end portion of a member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member in paragraphs [0070] and [0076] in conjunction with FIGs. 6A-6H and 7B (see page 6 of the Office Action).
Wolfe is generally directed to a neural probe that includes metallic traces along the length of the probe, where the metallic traces terminate at one or more contacts comprising nanosized metallic pillars (see, for example, the Abstract of Wolfe). Paragraph [0070] in conjunction with FIGS. 6A-6H of Wolfe describe a process flow for forming conductors (e.g., the metallic traces) and vias. Wolfe discloses that a probe needle may be coated with a multi-layer coating, such as a crosslinked PPMMA coating, sputtered gold 60, and a PPMMA resist 55. After forming gold traces 75 using a stencil mask 65, the unexposed resist is removed. A second PPMMA coating 85 is applied and crosslinked, and the probe is coated with an insulating coat except for an opening 95 (via) at the end of the gold trace where electrical contact is made to the cerebrospinal fluid.
Paragraph [0070] in conjunction with FIGS. 6A-6H of Wolfe therefore merely describe the fabrication of the metallic (e.g., gold) traces along the length of the probe that terminate at the opening (via) such that the metallic pillars at the end of the metallic traces are configured to make electrical contact with cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting device would have had the following layers: (i) a rigid material (e.g., shape memory alloy, stainless steel, titanium, glass) (see, for example, paragraph [0062] of Wolfe); (ii) a first crosslinked PPMMA coating; (iii) a gold metallic trace; (iii) a second crosslinked PPMMA coating; and (iv) an insulating coating, with an opening (via) through the second crosslinked PPMMA coating and the insulating coating to access the gold metallic trace.
There is no indication or suggestion in paragraph [0070] and FIGS. 6A-6H of Wolfe, however, that a particle is attached to the end portion of a member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member. Instead, the gold metallic trace and any nanosized metallic pillars in Wolfe are positioned internally, i.e., under the second crosslinked PPMMA coating and the insulating coating, such that the cerebrospinal fluid enters the opening (via) through the second crosslinked PPMMA coating and the insulating coating to contact the gold metallic trace.
Paragraph [0076] in conjunction with FIG. 7B of Rylander show an illustrative implementation of a light guide. Paragraph [0076] states that core 105 of the lightguide 100 may include metal wires 125 that terminate at a nanostructure 130. There is no teaching or suggestion in paragraph [0076] or FIG. 7B of Wolfe, however, that a particle is attached to the end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member. Instead, FIG. 7B of Wolfe shows core 105 of the lightguide 100 terminating at a nanostructure 130, with no indication that an adhesive is positioned between the nanostructure and the end portion of the member.
In view of the above, there would have been no rational reason for a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine Rylander and Wolfe such that at least one particle would be attached to the end portion of the microneedle in Rylander, since Wolfe fails to teach or suggest at least one particle attached to the end portion of the neural probe via an adhesive positioned between the at least particle and the end portion of the probe.
IV. There would have been no reasonable expectation of success in modifying Rylander such that at least one particle would be attached to the end portion of the microneedle via an adhesive.
The Examiner alleges that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have had motivation to combine Rylander and Wolfe with a reasonable expectation of success since Wolfe teaches that gold on the neural probe employs surface enhancement to boost signal detection of the neural probe, and Rylander and Wolfe both teach a member configured to guide and/or direct light (see page 7 of the Office Action). However, this rationale ignores the fact that the microneedles in Rylander are configured to penetrate skin, and thus, the particle would be removed or "scraped" from the microneedle as the microneedle is inserted into skin.
As described above, Rylander is generally directed to a minimally-invasive fiber optic microneedle that physically penetrates tissue to deliver light directly into a target area below the skin surface (see, for example, the Abstract of Rylander). The microneedles in Rylander are configured to penetrate skin up to a 1 mm depth to bypass the epidermal layer of skin, which scatters most light (see, for example, paragraph [0172] of Rylander). Fig. 1 of Waghule (previously discussed), which shows that the skin consists of the stratum corneum (10-40 micrometers), the epidermis (50-150 micrometers) and the dermis (1.5-4 mm), is reproduced below as FIG. Since the microneedles in Rylander are configured pass through the epidermal layer, the microneedles must penetrate through the stratum corneum and the epidermis (e.g., a depth of at least 60-190 micrometers). Furthermore, the microneedles in Rylander are difficult to insert into the skin, and a support member (e.g., an elastomeric support medium) must be used for increasing the critical buckling force of the needles to fortify the needles for insertion into the skin (see, for example, paragraphs [0032], [0219], and [0228] of Rylander).
Given such penetration depths and forces, any particle attached to the end portion of the microneedle in Rylander would have been removed as the microneedle was inserted into the skin. Thus, there would have been no rational or logical reason for attaching a particle to the end portion of the microneedle of Rylander. Instead, the reasonable expectation would have been that attaching any particle to the end portion of the microneedle of Rylander would have been a futile exercise, since there would have been no way to prevent the particle from being removed or scraped from the microneedle as the microneedle is inserted into human skin.
A person of ordinary skill in the art, looking to modify the microneedles disclosed in Rylander, would most certainly look to the plethora of literature directed to transdermal microneedles, not to the disclosure of Wolfe directed to neural probes or the disclosure of Sai directed to bent optical fibers. An example of such literature is Alimardani, V., et al., J. Clin. Med., 2021, 10, 181 ("Alimardani"), submitted herewith. Alimardani is a review article describing advancements in the application of microneedles for effective transdermal delivery of nanoparticles for a wide range of therapeutics in cancer chemotherapy and immunotherapy (see, for example, the Abstract of Alimardani). Sections 3.3 and 3.4 of Alimardani describe microneedle-assisted nanoparticle delivery in photothermal therapy and photodynamic therapy, respectively (see, for example, pages 10-13 of Alimardani), which are the therapeutic approaches used in Rylander for destruction of tumor cells (see, for example, paragraph [0161] of Rylander). Nowhere does Alimardani describe, however, attaching a particle to the end portion of a transdermal needle. This is unsurprising, as a person of ordinary skill in the art would have readily recognized that attaching a particle to the end portion of a transdermal needle would result in the particle being removed or scraped off as the needle was inserted into skin.
For example, Alimardani describes several strategies for delivering macromolecules across the skin, including a "coat-and-poke" approach, which consists of a microneedle coated with a water-soluble drug that dissolves within the skin during its administration (see, for example, page 3 of Alimardani in conjunction with Figure 2). Rohan, S.J., et al., J. Pharmacol. Exp. Ther., 2019, 370, 555-569, also submitted herein, is a review article that describes such coated microneedles (see, for example, the Abstract and Fig. 1 of Rohan). A person of ordinary skill in the art, being knowledgeable about the state of the art, e.g., as described by Alimardani and Rohan, would have recognized that coating microneedles with drugs would have been used instead of attaching particles so as to avoid losing or scraping particles off the microneedle as it is inserted into skin.
Accordingly, for at least these reasons, there would have been no rational reason to combine Rylander with Wolfe, since there would have been no way to keep the particles on the microneedle in such a combination.
V. Conclusion
As discussed above, the Examiner's selection of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai to reject the claims is based on impermissible hindsight, using the teachings of the instant specification as a road map, and is not based on the disclosure of the cited references as they would have been considered by a person of ordinary skill in the art. See M.P.E.P. § 2145(X)(A). A person of ordinary skill in the art, reading Rylander and seeking to modify it, would have looked to other transdermal needles, of which there are a plethora, and certainly not to the near-field scanning optical microscope of Hollingsworth, the neural probe of Wolfe, or the bent optical fiber of Sai, none of which are reasonably related to the field of transdermal needles.
Thus, for at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai does not render independent claim 1 obvious, and independent claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, or Sai, alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-138, 140- 144, 147, and 148, as asserted by the Examiner. Withdrawal of the claim rejections of this ground is respectfully requested, for at least the above-described reasons.
Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in view of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jung
Dependent claim 139 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Hollingsworth, in view of Sai, in view of Wolfe, and further in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2015/0092191 to Jung et al. ("Jung").
Claim 139 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai for at least the reasons outlined above. Jung fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 139 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jung. In addition, it is not conceded that Jung teaches any of the features recited in claim 139, and is it not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Jung in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejection on this ground is respectfully requested.
Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in view of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Hielme
Dependent claim 145 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Hollingsworth, in view of Sai, in view of Wolfe, and further in view of U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2003/0112443 to Hjelme et al. ("Hjelme").
Claim 145 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai for at least the reasons outlined above. Hjelme fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, and Sai noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 145 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Hjelme. In addition, it is not conceded that Hjelme teaches any of the features recited in claim 145, and is it not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Hollingsworth, Wolfe, Sai, and Hjelme in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejection on this ground is respectfully requested.
New Claims
New claims 149-151 depend from independent claim 1, which is believed to be patentable over the cited references for at least the reasons noted above. Thus, new claims 149-151 are also patentable over the cited references for at least the reasons noted above. In addition, new claims 149-151 recite features related to the adhesive or the cell that further distinguish the cited references.
CONCLUSION
In view of the foregoing remarks, this application should now be in condition for allowance. A notice to this effect is respectfully requested. If the Examiner believes, after the foregoing remarks, that the application is not in condition for allowance, the Examiner is requested to call the undersigned at 617-646-8000.
If this response is not considered timely filed and if a suitable request for an extension of time is otherwise absent, any necessary extension of time is hereby requested. If there is a fee occasioned by this response, including an extension fee, the Director is hereby authorized to charge any deficiency or credit any overpayment in the fees filed, asserted to be filed or which should have been filed herewith to Deposit Account No. 23/2825, under Docket No. H0498.70497US01, from which the undersigned is authorized to draw.
